result.markdown: --- title: "Session 5 — MNAR Sensitivity Analysis and Reporting" subtitle: "Delta adjustment · tipping point · Rubin's rules by hand · reporting missing data · Lab 5" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Sessions 3 and 4: MI under **MAR** - Today: **HbA1c** is missing for 21% of the adults, and the **high values** are the ones that go missing (**MNAR**) - By the end you can: - show why **MAR imputation cannot fix** MNAR - run a **delta-adjustment** sensitivity analysis and a **tipping point** - **report** missing data properly ::: # Topic 1 — The MNAR problem {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Observed vs MAR imputation ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} obs <- mean(dat$hba1c, na.rm = TRUE) mar <- summary(pool(with(imp, lm(hba1c ~ 1))))$estimate round(c(observed = obs, MAR_imputation = mar), 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` observed MAR_imputation 5.35 5.38 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} **5.35%** observed and **5.38%** after MAR imputation. The **truth is 5.50%** (known only because the data are synthetic). Adults with a **high HbA1c** did not come to the lab, and **nothing in the data says so**: MAR imputation learns from the **observed** (lower) values. ::: # Topic 2 — Delta adjustment {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Assume the missing values are higher ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} post <- make.post(dat2) post["hba1c"] <- "imp[[j]][, i] <- imp[[j]][, i] + 0.2" imp_d <- mice(dat2, m = 30, maxit = 10, seed = 2038, post = post, printFlag = FALSE) round(summary(pool(with(imp_d, lm(hba1c ~ 1))))$estimate, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5.42 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - **Delta** = the amount (here 0.2 percentage points) **added to every imputed HbA1c** to say: *"the missing values are on average higher by delta than a MAR model predicts"* - A **pattern-mixture** idea, done with `post` in `mice`: after each imputation step, **shift** the values - delta = 0 is **MAR**; delta > 0 is **MNAR** ::: ## A tipping-point table ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} run_delta <- function(delta) { po <- make.post(dat2); po["hba1c"] <- paste0("imp[[j]][, i] <- imp[[j]][, i] + ", delta) i <- mice(dat2, m = 20, maxit = 5, seed = 2038, post = po, printFlag = FALSE); s <- summary(pool(with(i, lm(hba1c ~ 1)))); c(delta = delta, mean = s$estimate, se = s$std.error) } do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8), run_delta)) |> round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` delta mean se [1,] 0.0 5.377 0.009 [2,] 0.2 5.422 0.010 [3,] 0.4 5.466 0.011 [4,] 0.6 5.508 0.012 [5,] 0.8 5.550 0.013 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} The mean rises by about **0.045 for each 0.2** (a fifth of the values are missing). With **delta of about 0.55** we reach the **true value 5.50**. In practice you **do not know the truth**: show **a range of plausible deltas** (from clinical knowledge) and ask **at which delta does my conclusion change?** (the **tipping point**). ::: ## Which conclusions are fragile? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} prev <- function(i) mean(sapply(1:i$m, function(k) mean(complete(i, k)$hba1c >= 6.5))) po5 <- make.post(dat2); po5["hba1c"] <- "imp[[j]][, i] <- imp[[j]][, i] + 0.5" imp_5 <- mice(dat2, m = 20, maxit = 5, seed = 2038, post = po5, printFlag = FALSE) round(100 * c(MAR = prev(imp), delta_0.5 = prev(imp_5)), 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` MAR delta_0.5 0.4 3.1 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} The share with **HbA1c of 6.5% or more** is **0.4%** under MAR (the same as the observed 0.4%) and **3.1%** with delta = 0.5 (the facilitator truth: **4.4%**). The **mean** moved a little; the **prevalence** of the high range moved **eightfold**. Conclusions about **tails** are the most **sensitive** to MNAR. ::: # Topic 3 — Rubin's rules and reporting {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Rubin's rules by hand ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fits <- with(imp, lm(hba1c ~ 1)) est <- sapply(fits$analyses, coef); vr <- sapply(fits$analyses, \(f) vcov(f)[1, 1]) m <- length(est); W <- mean(vr); B <- var(est) c(estimate = mean(est), W = W, B = B, total_se = sqrt(W + (1 + 1 / m) * B)) |> signif(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` estimate W B total_se 5.379e+00 7.784e-05 1.314e-05 9.561e-03 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.eq} T = W + (1 + 1/m) B W = mean within-imputation variance B = variance of the m estimates ::: ## Reporting missing data ::: {.good} - The **amount** of missing data **per variable**, and the number of **complete cases** - The **assumed mechanism** and the **reasons** (what you know) - The **method** (MICE, `pmm`), **m**, iterations, **variables in the imputation model** (outcome, auxiliary), software - **Pooled** estimates (Rubin's rules) and a **comparison with complete-case** - A **sensitivity analysis** for MNAR (delta, tipping point) - Follow **STROBE**/**TRIPOD**/**CONSORT** items on missing data ::: ::: {.key} *Example:* "Missing values (BMI 26%, HbA1c 21%, activity 12%, smoking 9%, SBP 6%) were handled by multiple imputation by chained equations (20 imputations, predictive mean matching, outcome and auxiliary variables in the imputation model, estimates pooled by Rubin's rules); a delta-adjustment sensitivity analysis explored departures from missing at random for HbA1c." ::: ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 5 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `missing-workshop/labs/lab5_mnar.R` - observed vs MAR-imputed mean HbA1c - delta adjustment, tipping-point table - Rubin's rules by hand, prevalence under MNAR, methods sentence ::: **Time:** 40 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="m5q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="1ipef5.afi4jp" data-show="SXQgbGVhcm5zIGZyb20gb2JzZXJ2ZWQgdmFsdWVzLCBzbyBpdCBjYW5ub3Qga25vdyB0aGUg bWlzc2luZyBvbmVzIGFyZSBoaWdo" data-explain="QSBNQVIgaW1wdXRhdGlvbiBtb2RlbCBpcyBlc3RpbWF0ZWQgb24gb2JzZXJ2ZWQgdmFsdWVz LiBJZiB0aGUgbWlzc2luZ25lc3MgZGVwZW5kcyBvbiB0aGUgdW5vYnNlcnZlZCB2YWx1ZSBp dHNlbGYsIG5vdGhpbmcgaW4gdGhlIGRhdGEgY29ycmVjdHMgZm9yIGl0Lg=="} Why does MAR imputation barely change the mean HbA1c (5.35 to 5.38) when it is the high values that are missing? - The imputation used too few iterations to reach the high values in the data - pmm cannot impute values larger than the observed mean of the variable in the data - It learns from observed values, so it cannot know the missing ones are high - MNAR data need to be removed from the dataset before the imputation starts ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="m5q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="1iprnt.afij11" data-show="U2hpZnRpbmcgaW1wdXRlZCB2YWx1ZXMgYnkgYSBjaG9zZW4gYW1vdW50IHRvIGV4cHJlc3Mg TU5BUg==" data-explain="RGVsdGEgaXMgdGhlIGFzc3VtZWQgYXZlcmFnZSBkaWZmZXJlbmNlIGJldHdlZW4gbWlzc2lu ZyBhbmQgb2JzZXJ2ZWQtbGlrZSB2YWx1ZXMuIGRlbHRhID0gMCBpcyBNQVIsIGFuZCBsYXJn ZXIgdmFsdWVzIGV4cHJlc3Mgc3Ryb25nZXIgZGVwYXJ0dXJlcy4="} What is a delta adjustment? - Dividing the pooled estimate by the fraction of missing information in it - Shifting imputed values by a chosen amount to express MNAR - Replacing the imputed values by the difference between two imputations - Adding the between-imputation variance to the standard errors of the estimates ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="m5q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="1iq4wj.afixif" data-show="SG93IGxhcmdlIG11c3QgZGVsdGEgYmUgYmVmb3JlIHRoZSBjb25jbHVzaW9uIGNoYW5nZXM/ " data-explain="VGlwcGluZy1wb2ludCBhbmFseXNpcyB2YXJpZXMgdGhlIE1OQVIgYXNzdW1wdGlvbiBhbmQg ZmluZHMgdGhlIHZhbHVlIGF0IHdoaWNoIHRoZSBzdWJzdGFudGl2ZSBjb25jbHVzaW9uIHdv dWxkIGNoYW5nZSwgc28gcmVhZGVycyBjYW4ganVkZ2Ugd2hldGhlciBpdCBpcyBwbGF1c2li bGUu"} The pooled mean HbA1c is 5.38 for delta = 0 and 5.55 for delta = 0.8. What does a tipping-point analysis ask? - What is the smallest delta that gives a significant result? - Which imputation method gives the highest estimate of the mean? - How large must delta be before the conclusion changes? - How many imputations does each delta need to converge? ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="m5q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="1iqi59.afjbzt" data-show="U29tZSByZXN1bHRzIGFyZSBzZW5zaXRpdmUgdG8gdGhlIE1OQVIgYXNzdW1wdGlvbiwgc28g c2hvdyBhIHJhbmdl" data-explain="RXN0aW1hdGVzIG9mIHRhaWxzIGFuZCBwcmV2YWxlbmNlcyBjYW4gY2hhbmdlIGdyZWF0bHkg d2l0aCBhbiBNTkFSIGFzc3VtcHRpb24uIFJlcG9ydGluZyBhIHJhbmdlIG9mIHBsYXVzaWJs ZSBkZWx0YXMgZ2l2ZXMgYW4gaG9uZXN0IHBpY3R1cmUu"} The share with HbA1c of 6.5% or more is 0.4% under MAR and 3.1% with delta = 0.5. What is the lesson? - MAR imputation is correct, and delta = 0.5 is the wrong assumption - Delta adjustment should replace MAR imputation in all of the analyses - The prevalence cannot be estimated from data that have missing values - Some results are sensitive to the MNAR assumption, so show a range ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="m5q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="1iqvdv.afjqh3" data-show="QW1vdW50IHBlciB2YXJpYWJsZSwgbWVjaGFuaXNtLCBtZXRob2QsIG0gYW5kIGEgc2Vuc2l0 aXZpdHkgYW5hbHlzaXM=" data-explain="UmVhZGVycyBuZWVkIHRvIGtub3cgaG93IG11Y2ggaXMgbWlzc2luZywgd2h5LCBob3cgaXQg d2FzIGhhbmRsZWQsIHdpdGggd2hhdCBzZXR0aW5ncywgYW5kIGhvdyByb2J1c3QgdGhlIGNv bmNsdXNpb25zIGFyZSB0byB0aGUgYXNzdW1wdGlvbi4="} What should a report say about missing data? - Amount per variable, mechanism, method, m and a sensitivity analysis - The p-value of Little's test together with the number of complete cases - The number of adults who were excluded from the study for missing data - The imputed values for each of the adults in the study, in a table ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - MAR imputation **cannot repair MNAR** - **Delta adjustment**: shift imputed values; delta = 0 is MAR - **Tipping point**: the delta at which the conclusion changes - Tails and prevalences are the most **sensitive** - Report **amount, mechanism, method, m, variables, pooling and sensitivity** ::: **Next:** Cheat sheet and the next module

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
